en: Another important term related to smart AI
systems built on top of large language
models, so typically AI agents, is the
concept of memory. Now,
I already mentioned that you may want to
ground model responses in sources, in web
sources or on PDF documents, for example,
that you may also have maybe a knowledge
database for a RAG approach to automatically
find relevant sources in that database.
But it's also quite important, at least in a
lot of scenarios, that your model, your AI
tool, remembers things,
remembers your preferences, your decisions,
or maybe past results.
The problem is, by default, large language
models can't remember anything. They are
just text in, text out. They don't have an
internal brain or memory or database or
anything like that. Instead, you and your
tools, which communicate with those large
language models need to provide all these
building blocks. Hence the external vector
database that may be needed for a RAG
approach.
Memory is something different though. You
could implement it with help of a vector
database too, but quite often memory simply
is also a bunch of text files, a bunch of
markdown files potentially, which may be
stored in
your
project folder in which you work with a
large language model, for example, where the
large language model or specifically the AI
agent or the tool that's driving the model
may
write certain key pieces of memory you want
to memorize for future sessions. And how
that works is in different ways. For
example, you could ask the model to memorize
something and it may then output tokens that
describe the thing that should be memorized.
And the tool that talks to the model then
goes ahead and writes that to a file. And
then the tool would also make sure that that
memory file is loaded and sent in
conjunction with your prompt to the large
language model for every future interaction
so that the large language model sees your
prompt plus any stored memory. That would be
one quite common way of ensuring that models
remember things or know about past
decisions. That is the idea. You can then
also differentiate between short-term and
long-term memory, or maybe you also have
certain memory files that belong to a
specific project and other memory files
that, files that are cross-project and
therefore sit in some global place on your
system. Or as mentioned, you could also look
into using databases, potentially vector
databases for efficient retrieval for
storing that memory. Because of course, the
boundary between memory and a general
knowledge base is kind of blurry. So all
these concepts are therefore related. But
it's definitely also quite common to use
very simple solutions and just store memory
in plain text file and simply attach all the
memory that could matter instead of finding
the very specific memory that's more likely
to matter
and inject all that memory with every
prompt. That is something you'll see in
quite a lot of projects.
